# Techniques at the easel

How the oil painter's techniques are done with this easel's tools, and the
traps that cost a painting time. `notes/easel_guide.md` says what each tool
does; this says how to use them. What you paint is yours to choose.

## Plan before you paint

- **Try it on the scratch canvas** (`scratch: true`): a mix, a stroke, a
  glaze, a wipe. Lay the underlayer it will go over, let it dry as long as
  it has on the painting, and compare the trial with the passage in a detail
  crop. Then paint it on the painting with the same pile and the same
  handling.
- **Plan in values.** `look` with `mode: "value,squint"` shows the picture as
  big masses of light and dark. Make the masses hold there first; the
  detail is built over them.
- **Coordinates.** A look's pixels are not canvas units. Use `grid: true` (or
  a crop with `grid: 10`) to read positions off a look before you aim a mask
  at something you saw.
  `mask: "<name>"` shows a global mask's outline and a light fill over
  the view; several names may be comma-separated.

## Before another pass: a decision checklist

1. **Check the paint state.** Use `drying(x, y)` along the next pass and
   at its edges: `"open"` blends and lifts; `"setting"` is stiff and barely
   blends; `"tacky"` has set and grabs the brush; `"dry"` is touch-dry.
   The call reads the top film. Where no wet paint lies, as in a gap
   between strokes, it reads the set layer beneath. A set layer under wet
   paint can still be tacky and grab the brush, so read a nearby gap too.
   Lay into open paint when you want strokes to fuse; wait for it to set
   when you want them separate. If tacky paint breaks the stroke, wait
   longer. See the guide's [Time](easel_guide.md#time).
2. **Diagnose a failed deposit in a detail crop.** Check the load, the
   paint the brush passed through and the layer beneath.
   - Gaps between marks: if the brush runs dry, use shorter strokes and
     reload more often. If gaps remain, check brush contact and coverage;
     extra coverage can add dabs and relief.
   - A continuous thin film showing the undercolor: test less thinning,
     a fuller deposit or a mixture with stronger hiding. Evidence for
     these fixes is limited, so compare them on the scratch canvas first.
   - A mixture changed by paint carried on the brush: use a fresh brush.
     If open underpaint caused the pickup and you want separate color,
     wait for it to set. Check the pile itself before changing its recipe.
3. **Prepare a transition.** Mix a few in-between tones, lay them and
   look. Blend while the paint is open, as [Blending](#blending) describes,
   and stop at the signs listed there. In dry paint, build the transition
   with new paint.
4. **Choose a repair.** If further handling keeps mixing an unsuccessful
   wet deposit, scrape or lift it before restating it. The knife scrapes
   wet paint down to set paint; the rag lifts it and leaves a thin
   tint. Inspect what remains before repainting. See
   [The knife](#the-knife) and [The rag](#the-rag) for handling and limits.
5. **Test a doubtful change.** Use the scratch procedure in
   [Plan before you paint](#plan-before-you-paint), matching the underpaint
   and its drying state. Change one condition, compare the results and
   carry the handling that worked over to the painting. Leave the passage
   alone if another pass has no clear benefit.

## Ground

- An **oil ground** (the default) absorbs nothing: paint stays open and
  glossy longer. An **absorbent ground** (`absorbent=true`) drinks the oil of
  thin paint: matte, lean, quick to set, colors that sit on the surface;
  thick paint stays open and glossy on top, and coarse pigments sink
  further than fine ones. Choose before you start: it is the
  canvas's character.
- A **toned ground** (a little ochre, umber or black in the white) sets the
  middle value from the first stroke; a white ground keeps everything high
  in key and lets thin paint glow.

## Lay-in: lean, quick, thin

- Thin the paint with turpentine (`pile{..., turps=0.6}`) for the first
  drawing and masses: it flows, covers fast and leaves a thin film that
  dries before the next sitting.
- **Fat over lean.** Each layer should be at least as oily as the one under
  it: lay-in lean (turpentine, blotted), body as from the tube, glazes rich
  (medium). Lean over fat dries matte and patchy over a still-soft layer.

## The whole picture, every time

- **Step back after every campaign** and ask whether the whole picture still
  does what you meant it to, as well as whether the last thing you fixed is
  fixed. Then `survey` it at full detail: what you can't see in a whole view
  is still on the canvas.
- **Values.** Check `mode: "value,squint"`: do the large lights, middles
  and darks give the effect you want? Light reads against darks; a high-key
  picture can keep a narrow range on purpose.
- **Light relationships.** Relate the light and shadow of each passage to
  the effect you want. A uniform band or a firm boundary can serve the
  picture; judge it against the whole.
- **Forms meet through relationships.** Overlap, color and edge handling
  separate or connect adjacent planes. A boundary that is only a mask's
  edge leaves their spatial relationship unstated.
- **Composition**: judge how the masses work together for the effect you
  chose. Where the emphasis sits, central or off-center, is yours to
  choose.

## Marks

- **A hierarchy of marks.** A few large decisive strokes (`b:gesture`), many
  middle ones, some small accents. One stroke size and one shape over a whole
  area reads as texture.
- **Mark scale and distance.** Marks that shrink through a passage
  (`scale_at`) can suggest recession; marks of similar scale throughout
  can compress depth.
- **Mark direction and form.** Direction can turn with a plane or bind
  neighboring planes through a shared rhythm. Strokes that wander in
  every direction read as noise.
- **Light and texture.** Bright light reads as light with soft edges and
  little texture. Busy or outlined strokes inside it, or strokes circling
  a center, turn it into an object.

## Spatter

- **Flicked paint makes scattered marks.**
  `b:spatter{at={x, y}, toward={dx, dy}}` throws droplets whose sizes,
  spacing and colors vary by themselves: aim the flick and let the droplets
  fall.
- **Thin the paint to make it fly**: a pile with medium or turpentine
  spatters; blotted paint hardly does. A hard flick gives a fine spray, a
  gentle one fat drops.
- **Mask what must stay clean** with `clip=`: droplets fly past any edge.
- A few flicks over a passage, then look.

## Forms and shadows

- **A form can read as one mass.** Relate its parts through color and
  overlap so they hold together. `form{}` gives a lit-volume guide, and
  color modulation builds solidity with or without that lighting.
- **Shadows take color from surrounding light.** With warm light reflected
  up near its base and cooler light from above, a shadow is warmer near its
  base and cooler above. Grade it in separate passes with different `pile=`
  values, and judge its value and temperature against the object casting
  it and the passages around it. One violet for every shadow is the usual
  trap.
- **Distance and color.** Distance lightens and cools: far forms are paler
  and bluer than near ones and closer to each other in tone. Similar
  intensity in near and far planes can compress depth.

## The palette

- **Look at the board before the canvas.** `look` with `palette: true` shows
  each heap thick and thinned over black: a chalky mix, a violet "gray", a
  glaze that stains or one that hides show there, before they cost a passage.
- **Steer a mix by eye**: `p:add{}` a touch at a time, looking between
  additions.
- **Matching a passage** for a repair: start from its recipe in the log and
  lay a trial beside it. The layers since may have shifted the passage, so
  judge the laid trial in a detail crop.
- **Set out a limited palette** for a picture that should hang together; a
  few tubes mixed every way give related colors by themselves.
- **A dirty board unifies.** `palette{dirty=0.2}` to `0.4` lets each heap
  pick up a trace of the others through a sitting, as a working palette does;
  clean it (`palette{clean=true}`) when a passage needs pure color.

## Broken color

- **Many close piles.** Knife three to five piles of neighboring colors
  (warmer, cooler, lighter, darker) and lay them as separate strokes over
  the same area; the eye mixes them. `mix_jitter=` in `work` varies each
  dip; every pile is a little uneven.
- **Two colors on one brush.** `b:load(p, 0.8); b:load(p2, 0.5, {side=1, share=0.4})`, or
  `work(m, {pile=p, second={pile=p2, side=1, share=0.45}})`: each stroke carries both,
  side by side, mingling as it goes. `streak=` loads unevenly, in bands.
- **Wet into wet.** A stroke dragged through wet paint picks some of it up
  and carries it along: color changes within the stroke. Work an area while
  it is open (`drying(x, y)` says "open") for soft transitions; wait for it
  to set for crisp, separate strokes on top.
- **Watch the white.** Every pile with much lead white is chalky. Keep white
  for the lights; let the darks and middles be pigment.
- **Corrections stay close in value.** Keep a correction within a value step
  of what surrounds it, and small accents near their surroundings' value: a
  thin pale accent against a dark reads as a crack.
- **Vary the touch.** One stroke length and one brush over a whole canvas
  reads as a mechanical texture. Change brush size, stroke length, direction
  and pressure from passage to passage; leave some passages quiet.

## Impasto

- **Thick paint for lights and accents.** Most of a canvas is thin: lay-in and shadows
  lean (turpentine), middle tones as from the tube. Keep the thick, blotted
  paint for the lights and the accents. Impasto everywhere reads as flat.
  `load_at=` varies the load across a pass; `scale_at` gives ridges of
  different sizes.

- Stiff paint holds the brush's marks: blot it (`pile{..., blot=0.3}`) or
  use it as it comes from the tube, with no medium. A full brush lays more with `lay=4`
  to `lay=16`; a coarse hog brush (larger `hair`) leaves coarser ridges.
- In stiff paint the hairs gather into clumps: strokes lie in ridges and
  furrows, walls rise along their sides, a bead where they end. Fluid paint
  levels flat, which suits a glaze.
- Check it with `look` and `mode: "relief"` (raking light from the upper
  left at 25°: it exaggerates, as a raking lamp does) and with
  `mode: "gallery"` (55°, as the picture is seen on a wall). Judge the
  picture under the gallery light; use raking light to inspect the surface.
- Let impasto set before painting into it, unless you want the new stroke
  to drag the old one along.

## The knife

- `k = knife{width=30}; k:load(p, 1.0); k:lay(points, {pressure={0.5, 0.5}})`
  lays a slab with a flat top, torn where it parts from the blade (its ends,
  its leading edge): light pressure lays it thick, and the paint runs out
  sooner; firm pressure thin, and it goes further. The points set its path.
- Pulled lightly over **dry** impasto, it catches only the ridges: broken
  color over a textured underlayer, a sparkle of light paint on dark.
- `k:scrape(points, {pressure=1})` takes wet paint off down to what is dry:
  to restate a passage, or to leave a ghost of it.

## Blending

- **Blend inside one passage.** Shape the mask like the passage, with its
  edge where the paint already matches. Keep everything you want to keep
  outside the mask, dry shapes included: the blender carries wet paint onto
  them.
- **Look after each pass.** The blender lifts paint as it moves it. When
  darks go pale, texture flattens or the weave shows through, stop.
- **A seam that keeps coming back** needs another method. A smaller patch
  blended again rebuilds the box. Try something else across the whole
  transition on the scratch canvas: a thin tint of the original recipe,
  interlocking strokes of the two neighboring colors over dry paint, or the
  connected passage repainted up to its natural edges.

## Glazing and scumbling (over dry paint)

- **Glaze**: a transparent paint (lakes, viridian, ultramarine, a little of
  anything) with plenty of medium (0.7 to 0.85), `hand="glaze"`, over a dry
  passage. It deepens and saturates and lets the light underneath through;
  it rescues a chalky passage. Over impasto it pools in the valleys and
  thins on the ridges, which then shine through. Too much pigment, or any
  white, lays an opaque veil: try it small first. A glaze over the whole
  picture to pull it together has failed more often than it has worked.
- **Scumble**: light paint dragged thin over a dry darker passage, broken
  by the surface. A light load and
  `hand="scumble"` often lay opaque dabs. The veils that blended in came
  from paint thinned with `thinner`, laid in several light passes. Try it
  on the scratch canvas first.
- Glazes and scumbles want the passage under them **dry** (`wait` until
  `drying` says so): over open paint they just mix.

## Keeping control

- **Clip** a pass near anything it must not touch (`clip=` a mask). The body
  hands carry paint past their mask's edge by as much as a stroke's length:
  without a clip they paint over what is next to them.
- **Protect what is there now.** Paint fine marks after the passages behind
  them where you can. In every later pass over that area, subtract each of
  them from the mask (`m - protected`), and subtract again after `grow` or
  `blur`, which spread the mask back over them.
- **Check a mask before painting through it**: `print(m:at(x, y))` at a few
  points inside the target and just outside it, past each end of a band.
- **Masks from earlier chunks**: a `local` mask is gone in the next chunk.
  Keep what later chunks need as globals: paths, recipes, protection masks.
  Before redrawing something by eye, look for its saved path. Keep big
  temporary masks local (memory).
- **Small forms** drawn as a neat diagram of separate parts can read as
  icons. A few thick, irregular touches of two or three colors read as the
  thing.
- **Taking paint off**: wet paint comes off with the rag (below) or the
  knife, down to the first set layer. Set paint stays: paint over it or
  glaze it. Either way it costs only painted time.

## The rag

- **It lifts wet paint down to the first set layer.** Earlier passes that
  haven't set are part of the same wet film, so a firm lift can take them
  too, down to set paint or the ground. Before a wipe, check
  `drying(x, y)` in the paint: `"open"` paint lifts, `"setting"` paint
  comes away slowly, and `"tacky"` or `"dry"` paint has set and stays.
  A wipe usually leaves a thin wet tint, and `drying(x, y)` reads that
  tint as `"open"` or `"setting"`. If the tint is `"setting"`, or the set
  layer under it is still tacky, it grabs the brush when you repaint.
  Check it at a nearby gap in the paint, where `drying(x, y)` reads the
  set layer.
- **Dip it for a lift.** A dry rag lifts less and leaves a pale tint of
  the color in the weave: useful for wiping lights out of a wet glaze or
  lay-in. To take a passage off, dip well (`r:dip(0.9)`), press firmly,
  give it two or three passes, then go over it again across the first
  direction with a fresh, dipped rag.
- **The spirits go in minutes.** Dampness halves every three minutes of
  painting time, and a long mask wipe takes minutes. Dip just before each
  wipe; `print(r.damp)` says how much is left.
- **A face fills up.** `print(r.load)`: near 1, the face lifts almost
  nothing, and the reply says so when a wipe ran on a full face. Refold
  (`refold=` in a mask wipe); when `r.soaked` nears 1 the whole cloth is
  full, so take a fresh rag. A wide wet area fills a face fast.
- **A mask wipe stays inside its mask.** Paint outside the mask is left as
  it was. A path wipe has no mask: the whole pad lifts, so along an edge
  you need crisp, use a rag narrower than the strip.
- **Shape the mask like the passage.** Mask wipes start and stop a little
  inside the mask, so a rectangle leaves a frame of the wiped color. If a
  frame shows, wipe along its sides with a path.
- **Expect a trace.** Even a good lift leaves a tint, streaks along the
  wipe or a rim where it stopped. Look at a detail crop before you call it
  clean, and before you paint over it. Thick paint takes many fresh, dipped
  wipes.
- **One lift, then a new plan.** If the same passage needs lifting twice,
  change what goes on it before painting it again.

## Time

- Time passes only as you paint or `wait`. Paint dries on its own clock:
  lead white and umber fast, lakes and vermilion slow, thin paint faster than
  thick. Added medium and the slower oils (walnut, poppy) slow it; an
  absorbent ground sets thin paint laid straight on it quickly.
- **Check `drying(x, y)` at several points** along the next pass, its edges
  included: thick and thin parts of one passage dry at different rates.
- A painting can take months of painted time. Let layers dry between
  campaigns; that is what lets the next one sit on top.

## Finishing

- An unvarnished picture keeps its matte and glossy passages as painted.
  A varnish (where the easel has one) makes it all glossy: darks deepen.

# Studio notes

Observations of the canvas, the paint and the tools at this easel, by
operation: what was done, what the paint did and, where it's known, why.
Each was seen under particular conditions and may be incomplete or wrong.
They describe how the easel behaves. Widths and positions are in canvas
units (the canvas is 1000 units wide).

## The canvas and ground

1. The linen's vertical threads are more even than the horizontal ones,
   which carry thick slubs a few millimeters long; their spacing follows the
   counts set in `canvas{}`.
2. The ground chosen in `canvas{}` shows through thin paint; body color
   hides it.
3. Light paint laid at light pressure over a wet dark catches only the high
   points of a knife-textured ground. The dark stays in the hollows as a
   net of fine dark lines that looks like cracking.
4. Bristles plow paint off the tops of the weave, so a lay-in can keep
   small specks of bare ground. A denser pass covers them.

## Paint in thin films

5. A coat of paint over paint of its own masstone looks the same at any
   thickness, so a mark from a pile matching what it lies on disappears
   into it.
6. A thin film looks different from its pile. Thin dark or earth mixtures over
   a pale passage come out lighter, warmer and more saturated than the
   masstone on the palette.
7. The thin fringe of an umber or black stroke over a light field dries
   as a warm brown to warm gray halo. A blue stroke's fringe stays blue.
8. Lead white hides strongly (its hiding in the guide's tube table is
   0.82; how much a coat covers also depends on its thickness). A thin veil
   of a pale lead-white mixture lies over what is under it and lightens it,
   like a scumble.

## Brushes

9. Every brush is blunt unless given a `point`. A blunt brush's mark runs
   from about half its width at the lightest touch to its full width pressed
   (a little more with splay), so it can't taper to a point.
10. A pointed brush at light pressure lays a hairline, and its width grows
    with pressure. A band a few units wide needs real pressure or a blunt
    brush of that width. A stroke whose pressure falls off at the end draws
    down to the tip and still reaches the end of its path.
11. A brush keeps its paint across strokes. Each stroke lays most at its
    start, and the load runs down along the stroke, so a long drag with a
    wide brush runs dry partway and leaves thinly covered streaks and bands.
12. A well-loaded hair wets the hollows of the weave. A nearly empty one
    skims the tops (dry brush, broken color). Soft hair bends down into the
    hollows; stiff bristle rides on the tops.
13. Whether a dry brush breaks up depends on its load, the pressure, the
    paint below and the ground's texture.
14. A pointed brush loaded below about a quarter stops wetting the hollows,
    and its thin line breaks up along the weave. Run dry, the tip loses its
    point and splits.
15. A pressed touch lays one continuous, nearly round patch (the paint
    bridges the hairs) that grows with pressure.

## Strokes, passes and clipping

16. `clip=true` stops every bristle on the mask's edge, weighted by the
    mask's value. A clipped fill reproduces the mask's outline exactly, as
    one even line, steps and corners included. The `detail` and `blend`
    hands are clipped by default; `broad`, `body`, `hatch`, `glaze` and
    `scumble` are unclipped.
17. Unclipped strokes run past the mask's edge by their own length and
    width. Along a long straight edge they throw small irregular patches into the field
    beyond, and a brush wider than a band spreads well outside it.
18. The square ends of unclipped strokes notch a shape's edge into steps.
19. In `work`, the mask's value decides where strokes are anchored (at or
    above `threshold`: 0.3, or 0.1 for `detail`). Unclipped, strokes end
    where their lengths end, however soft the mask's edge.
20. `work` leaves the ground showing between its strokes. With `fill=true`
    it looks at its passage afterward and dabs paint into the bare spots its
    strokes left. Single `stroke` and `touch` calls don't fill in.
21. Short strokes planned along a band about one unit wide come out as a
    dashed line: the planner lays them separately, with gaps.
22. Parallel strokes that all break at the same places leave a row of stroke
    ends across the passage, and the outer strokes' ends make a lobed edge.
23. `cut_in` with a round along a curved edge lays short strokes that follow
    it as a string of small bumps.
24. In a smooth lean passage, the loaded starts of broad strokes stay as
    lighter patches. Blending reduces them and leaves traces.

## Wet into wet

25. A brush over open paint lifts some of it and mixes it with its own. A
    clean brush lifts wet paint, less as it sets, and nothing from set or
    dry paint.
26. Light touches into a wet dark dissolve into it. The same touches on
    paint that has set stay where they land.
27. A pale stroke dragged through a wet dark picks up the dark and comes out
    streaked, grayer and less opaque, so what is underneath shows.
28. A dark stroke laid into a wet pale passage lifts the pale and comes out
    paler than its pile.
29. A passage laid against a wet neighbor drags the neighbor into its edge.
30. Crossing strokes in wet paint thin each other at the crossings, and the
    layer below shows there.
31. A tacky surface grabs: a brush dragged over it leaves its paint sooner
    and in broken patches (stick and slip).

## Stippling

32. Touches into a wet layer lift some of it and fuse. On a dry layer each
    touch stays separate.
33. One dip serves one small patch of touches (24 by default), and each
    dip's mixture varies a little. On a dry layer the passage can dry as a
    patchwork of slightly different patches; fewer touches per dip make the
    patches smaller.
34. Coverage is how many touches fall on each point; one touch covers about
    π(0.4 × width)².
35. Contrast with what is underneath decides how a stipple reads. A coverage
    that gives a veil over a mid tone gives solid patches over a pale field.
36. With `feather` above 0, touches press lighter where coverage falls
    below 1, so a thinning stipple ends in smaller, fainter marks; at 0 they
    keep their pressure.
37. A row of separate touches along a thin line reads as a string of beads.
    A short dragged stroke along it reads as one continuous ridge.

## Blending

38. The blender fuses open paint by lifting it and moving it. It can't move
    set or dry paint.
39. `blend` stays inside its mask by default. Unclipped, it drags wet paint
    across the mask's edge.
    A local blend can leave a seam where lifted or moved paint meets the
    untouched paint outside that mask. Inside a soft mask, wet dark and
    light passages still mix.
40. Touches stippled into a wet layer and then blended fuse into it. Only
    the strongest contrasts survive, as thin traces. Touches laid after the
    blending pass stay on top as a lacy texture.
41. Repeated blending of one lean layer lifts paint off the tops of the
    weave, and the ground shows through as a pale lattice.
42. Blending spreads each thin spot in a layer into a soft-edged patch.

## Glazing

43. A brushed glaze (`hand="glaze"`) is unclipped.

## Masks

44. Every mask covers the whole canvas. A mask function that stays above
    zero far from the spot you mean paints there too.
45. Masks from shapes (`poly`, `rect`, `ellipse`, `ribbon`) are crisp.
    `soften` and `blur` give them a ramp. `roughen` replaces the ramp with a
    new edge at the 0.5 level, so a long soft fade comes back as a hard
    edge.
46. `ribbon` puts a round disc at every point, both ends included, so it
    reaches half a width past its end points.
47. Two separately softened masks that meet leave a light gap or a dark
    overlap along the seam. A mask and its inverse (`m` and `-m`) meet
    without one.
48. A passage bounded by a mask shows a cut edge wherever its paint differs
    from its neighbor's at the mask's edge.

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting, tacky and touch-dry.
    Drying depends on pigment, thickness and oil; the guide describes
    the times at this easel.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers
    it.

# Wet-on-wet landscape painting: materials and technique for an oil-paint simulator

**Scope.** This note covers the fast alla prima landscape method, where a whole landscape is finished in one sitting and every layer goes into wet paint. It describes the ground, paint, tools, order of work and the physics that makes it hold together. Values tagged **[est]** are engineering guesses to tune, not measured figures.

---

## 1. Ground

- **Support:** a stretched, double-primed canvas, commonly 18×24 in (457×610 mm). The priming makes it nonabsorbent, so the wet ground stays open and the weave stands up through it.
- **Variants:** a black or gray gesso ground, left to dry fully, for night scenes and strong contrast. Contact paper or tape can mask a shape (an oval, a window) before the ground goes on, which gives a vignette with a clean edge.
- **Liquid white:** an oil white thinned with oil and a little solvent. One manufacturer's safety data sheet gives 1–10% hydrotreated heavy naphtha, density 1.2–1.6 g/cm³ and a flash point near 62 °C; the full recipe is unpublished. A home version of about one part titanium white to one part linseed oil is common but unverified. A liquid black (the same medium with carbon black) serves dark grounds, and a pigment-free liquid clear keeps the slip without lightening the colors laid into it.
- **Application:** a thin, even coat over the whole canvas with a wide flat brush, just enough to cover it. Painting starts while it is still wet. No thickness figure is published.
- **What it does:** colors laid into the wet ground slide and blend on the canvas, and brushing across it removes excess paint, so later layers go on easily. Each stroke also picks up some of the white, so color laid into liquid white comes out lighter. That is why the clear version exists.

## 2. Paint

**Palette.** A small fixed set of firm oils: titanium white, phthalo blue, prussian blue, phthalo green, alizarin crimson, a bright red, a cadmium-yellow hue, indian yellow, yellow ochre, sap green, dark sienna, van dyke brown, a chromatic black and a premixed mountain dark.

| Color | CI pigments | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Titanium white | PW6 | opaque |
| Phthalo blue | PB15:3 | very strong; it overwhelms crimson in a mix |
| Prussian blue | PB27 (some labels add PG178, PB198; **conflict**) |  |
| Phthalo green | PG7 |  |
| Alizarin crimson | PR83 | transparent |
| Bright red | PR255, PR254 | not cadmium |
| Cadmium yellow hue | PY74 | not cadmium |
| Indian yellow | PY83 |  |
| Yellow ochre | PY43 |  |
| Sap green | PY42, PY83, PG7 |  |
| Dark sienna | PBr7 |  |
| Van dyke brown | PBr7, PBk9 |  |
| Chromatic black | PR83, PG7 | a deep green-crimson, not a neutral black |
| Mountain dark | PB27, PBr7, PBk9, PR83, PG7 | premixed |

**Consistency:** the paint is far stiffer than ordinary tube oil, close to dry, and that firmness is what makes the method work. No viscosity or yield data are published.

**Thinning:** thinner goes on sparingly, a touch on the brush so the new paint is a little softer than the paint already on the canvas. Liner paint is thinned until it almost runs. The thinner is an odorless hydrocarbon solvent with kinematic viscosity at or below about 20 mm²/s.

## 3. Tools

The landscape brushes mix natural and synthetic bristle; the liner and the soft blender are natural bristle.

| Tool | Size and use and handling |
| --- | --- |
| **2-inch flat** | head ≈50 mm wide, hair ≈63 mm long. Skies, water and any large area. Loaded by tapping into the paint so only the top bristles carry it. Clouds: dab with one corner, then small circles with the brush on its side. Mist: tap the base of a shape with a clean, dry brush and lift gently upward. A brush wet with thinner thins the paint and turns it mushy. |
| **1-inch flat** | 25 mm. Base coats for clouds, water, mountains, trees and bushes; crisscross strokes at mountain bases for fog. |
| **1-inch oval** | Evergreens, foothills and highlights. |
| **#6 fan** | [est] 30–35 mm. Evergreens (heavily loaded on both sides), distant trees (the top corner only), grass (long flat strokes pushed upward, back and forth in a zigzag), trunks, foothills, boats. |
| **#3 fan** | [est] ~20 mm. The same marks, smaller and tighter. |
| **#6 filbert** | Trunks, waves and detail. |
| **Liner** | point [est] 1–2 mm. Loaded with thin paint, the bristles rolled to a sharp point. Twigs, fine branches and the signature. |
| **#10 knife** | straight blade ≈95×32 mm. Larger and stiffer than an ordinary painting knife, with a straight edge. Mountains. |
| **#5 knife** | smaller. Tight areas. |

**Knife loading:** paint is pressed out flat on the palette, then the knife edge cuts across it and picks up a thin bead of paint along the edge.

**Knife deposit:**
- **Mountain body:** the dark goes on firmly and the excess is scraped back, but not all of it. Scraping too much leaves too little dark for the highlights to read against.
- **Highlights:** almost no pressure. The bead glides over the dark and breaks on the texture, leaving gaps, and the gaps are what make it read as rock. Solid, even coverage looks like frosting.
- **Direction:** highlight and shadow strokes follow the slope of each face.
- **Scratching:** the knife point scratches in sticks and twigs.

**Cleaning:** the brush is washed in odorless thinner, then the excess is shaken and knocked out against something hard, so it goes back to the paint nearly dry.

## 4. Order of work

A winter lake scene shows the usual sequence:

1. Liquid white over the whole canvas with the 2-inch brush, left wet.
2. Sky: alizarin crimson crisscrossed low for a glow. Phthalo blue with the chromatic black above, crisscrossed all the way across the top, then blended downward without overworking.
3. Water: the same colors in horizontal strokes.
4. Mountain: the knife with a dark mix (prussian blue, chromatic black, van dyke brown, alizarin). The body is softened with the 1-inch brush and its base crisscrossed into fog.
5. Mountain highlights: a small bead of white on the lit side; white, phthalo blue and a little of the dark on the shadow side. Tap the base and lift for mist.
6. Background evergreens: the mountain dark plus a little white, on the fan brush.
7. Reflections: the 1-inch brush pulled straight down (an angled pull makes them look wrong), then light horizontal passes across. The water line: a very small bead of titanium white mixed with liquid white, cut in with the knife.
8. Foreground evergreens and bushes pushed up in dark. Scratched twigs.
9. Highlights: white, liquid white and a touch of blue, leaving some dark showing. Wipe the brush whenever it picks up dark.
10. Liner work and the signature.

**Timing:** a complete landscape takes about half an hour of painting time. Complex scenes have parts prepared beforehand.

## 5. Why wet-on-wet works physically

- **The rule:** thin paint sticks to thick paint. The first layers are the firmest; each later layer is slightly softer than what lies under it, so it can sit on top without sinking in.
- **Inference [est]:** stiff paint holds its shape on the thin wet film. A slightly more fluid paint then transfers onto it by adhesion without shearing the lower layer. If the top paint is stiffer, the brush lifts the lower layer instead. A stroke that will not stick gets a touch of thinner.
- **Pickup:** brushes lift wet color from underneath, so a brush that picks up dark is wiped before the next light stroke. Colors also mix on the brush itself: tap two colors in, then push.
- **Layer order:** dark before light and back before front. Broken light paint over dark lets the dark show through.

## 6. Motifs, composition and color schemes

**Usual subjects:** trees in almost every painting (evergreen and deciduous about equally, often with bushes); cumulus skies; mountains, often snowy; lakes and rivers, sometimes a waterfall or the sea; winter scenes; a cabin; occasionally an oval or half-oval vignette.

**Habits:**
- Trees come in pairs or clusters rather than alone.
- Clouds are light and rounded on top and nearly flat underneath.
- Distant trees get little detail, and some stay without highlights.
- Mountains fade into mist at the base, and lakes get vertical reflections plus a water line.
- Vignettes are masked with contact paper or tape.

**Color schemes:**
- **Skies:** phthalo blue over a crimson glow.
- **Mountains:** a dark mix with plenty of crimson, which gives the blue a lavender cast.
- **Foliage:** a blue-black-brown-crimson dark, highlighted with sap green plus cadmium yellow, yellow ochre or indian yellow, sometimes crimson or bright red.
- **Cabins:** van dyke brown and dark sienna, highlighted by grazing a bead of paint off the knife.

---

## Implications for a simulator

Every [est] value is a tunable guess; none is published.

1. **Rheology:**
   - Model paint as a yield-stress (Bingham or Herschel-Bulkley) fluid.
   - Firm colors: yield stress [est] 3–10× a soft tube oil.
   - Liquid grounds: near-Newtonian and thin.
   - Thinner lowers yield stress, and liner paint is near zero.
   - Density: 1.35–2.0 (colors) and 1.2–1.6 g/cm³ (grounds).
2. **Deposit rule:** transfer happens when tool-paint yield stress is at or below canvas-paint yield stress and contact pressure is low. Otherwise the tool picks up canvas paint. Mixing scales with shear and contact time.
3. **Liquid white:**
   - Thickness [est] 20–50 µm.
   - It stays wet all session, so no drying model is needed.
   - It lowers surface friction and adds white to each stroke.
   - Liquid black adds carbon black; liquid clear has no pigment.
4. **Canvas:** 18×24 in (457×610 mm), nonabsorbent and double-primed. Its weave peaks decide where knife paint breaks.
5. **Tools:**
   - 2-inch flat: 50×63 mm hair.
   - 1-inch flat: 25 mm.
   - #6 fan: [est] 30–35 mm. #3 fan: [est] ~20 mm.
   - Liner point: [est] 1–2 mm.
   - #10 knife: 95×32 mm straight edge.
   - Loading per side and per corner (a tap loads the top bristles only).
6. **Knife:**
   - The bead is [est] 1–2 mm along the edge.
   - Body mode: high pressure, full deposit, partial scrape.
   - Highlight mode: near-zero force, so paint transfers only at texture and paint peaks. Aim for [est] 30–70% broken fill, with more gaps at lower pressure.
   - Point scratch removes paint along a line.
7. **Strokes by motif:**
   - Sky: rows of X strokes, then horizontal blending downward.
   - Clouds: corner taps and small circles with flat bottoms, then a dry upward blend.
   - Mountain: knife ridge, 1-inch body blend, tap-and-lift mist.
   - Evergreen: a center line, then fan dabs widening downward.
   - Bushes: corner push-ups.
   - Grass: a fan brush pushed up in a zigzag.
   - Reflections: a vertical pull, light horizontal passes and a knife water line.
   - Twigs: liner or knife scratch.
8. **Order:** ground → sky → water tone → mountains (dark → highlight → mist) → background trees → reflections and water line → middle ground → foreground darks → highlights → twigs → signature.
9. **Optics:**
   - PB15:3, PG7 and PR83 are transparent and high-tinting; PW6 is opaque.
   - The chromatic black (PR83 + PG7) is not neutral.

# Physics of oil paint on canvas

**Tags.** **[V]**: the number is in the source text. **[S]**: the number is from a summary of the source. **[E]**: an estimate or derivation, with its assumptions stated.

---

## 1. Rheology and leveling

**Constitutive behavior.** Tube oil paint is a viscoplastic, shear-thinning and thixotropic suspension. A Herschel–Bulkley law fits it well: τ = τ_y + K·γ̇ⁿ, with n ≈ 0.2–0.7[S].

| Quantity | Value | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Yield stress, model ultramarine oil paint (32 vol% solids) | **10–20 Pa**. Brushstrokes came out regular and low-relief (Rz < 100 µm) | [V] |
| Yield stress, same paint + 4 vol% egg yolk (capillary network) | **≈3000–3200 Pa**. Strong impasto, and wrinkling suppressed | [V] |
| Typical tube paints | ~10–1000 Pa; stiff impasto grades above 1000 Pa | [S] |
| Apparent viscosity | 10⁴–10⁷ Pa·s at 0.01–0.1 s⁻¹; 10–10³ Pa·s at 10–100 s⁻¹ (brushing) | [S] |
| Linseed oil (the medium) | η ≈ 0.048 Pa·s, σ ≈ 33–36 mN/m at 20 °C | [S] |
| Stand oil | η ≈ 0.5–25 Pa·s depending on grade | [S] |

Impasto requires "sufficiently high yield stress preventing levelling after brush passage," while brushability depends on the *high-shear* viscosity, so stiff paint can still brush easily[V].

**Orchard leveling (Newtonian, thin film h ≪ λ).** A sinusoidal ridge of wavelength λ on a film of mean thickness h decays as a(t) = a₀·e^(−t/τ), with

  **τ = 3η(λ/2π)⁴ / (σh³)**[V].

The dependence is λ⁴ and h⁻³, so λ and h matter far more than η or σ.

**Yield-stress floor.** Surface tension produces a leveling stress of about 8π³σha/λ³. Flow stops once τ_y exceeds it, so ridges smaller than

  **a_c = τ_y λ³ / (8π³ σ h)**

stay frozen[S]. For thixotropic paint, τ_y(t) recovers after brushing, so leveling starts and then freezes with a residual mark[S]. With solvent evaporation, moderate yield stress can reduce residual unevenness[S].

**Worked numbers [E]** (σ = 0.035 N/m):

| Case | η | λ | h | τ (1/e time) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Medium-rich glaze, bristle striation | 1 Pa·s | 0.3 mm | 20 µm | 0.06 s |
| Glaze, stroke-scale ridge | 1 Pa·s | 2 mm | 20 µm | 110 s |
| Tube paint, stroke ridge, low-shear η | 10³–10⁴ Pa·s | 2 mm | 100 µm | 15 min – 2.5 h |

| τ_y | Frozen amplitude a_c, λ = 0.3 mm, h = 100 µm | a_c, λ = 2 mm, h = 300 µm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 15 Pa | ~0.5–1 µm | ~45 µm |
| 100 Pa | ~3–6 µm | ~300 µm |
| 500 Pa | ~15–30 µm | effectively frozen |
| 3000 Pa | ~90–200 µm | frozen |

The ranges come from comparing the thin-film form with a deep-layer form, a_c ≈ τ_yλ²/(4π²σ), derived for h ≳ λ/2π, where the lubrication assumption fails [E]. **Inferred for this case:** at the example's λ = 0.3 mm and h = 100 µm, the estimated arrest amplitude rises from about 0.5–1 µm at 15 Pa to about 3–6 µm at 100 Pa. Retained relief depends on wavelength, thickness, initial amplitude and recovering rheology, so no single yield stress marks where striations become visible. The Newtonian glaze example predicts that fine striations level quickly. Which marks stay visible also depends on conditions these calculations leave out.

## 2. Brush marks

| Fiber | Diameter | Tip | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hog bristle | 0.20–0.30 mm (fine hog 0.15–0.25) | Naturally split ("flagged") | [S] |
| Kolinsky/red sable | ~60–120 µm | Single fine taper | [S] |

In profilometry of oil paintings, the height features that best identify the painter sit at **0.2–0.4 mm**, matching the bristle widths used (**0.25 and 0.65 mm**)[V]. For macro impasto, a 17th-century canvas has measured relief up to about 0.85 mm[S].

**Dry brush and scumble.** A technical description of an 1879/80 canvas reports "an almost dry brush [dragged] across the surface, catching only the thread tops". This works even over a heavy, smooth ground: the paint goes where the brush touches.

## 3. Film formation and drying

- **Mass and skin timeline.** A titanium white in alkali-refined linseed oil (10 mil ≈ 250 µm film) gained nearly **16%** of its oil weight in the first days. It "begins to skin over" as it nears the peak and is touch-dry at **4–6 days**. Cold-pressed and alkali-refined oils peak at **15–18%** and then slowly lose mass over a year or more[V].
- **Thickness.** Thicker oil-paint films generally take longer to dry. Drying also depends on pigment, oil and additives. The easel guide describes drying in this studio.
- **Induction.** Drying oils take up oxygen only after an induction period; driers shorten it or speed the uptake. Lead white alone barely speeds the oxidation of linseed oil, and its impurities (litharge, lead acetate) probably account for its reputation as a drier[S].
- **Skinning and wrinkling.** Oxygen enters through the surface, so a crosslinked skin forms over mobile paint. Wrinkling is a compressive buckle of that skin. It is worse in thick, oil-rich or drier-heavy films[V]. Raising τ_y to about 3200 Pa suppressed wrinkling in model paints[V].
- **Long-term shrinkage and brittleness** (films 21–31 years old, cold-pressed linseed oil)[S]:

| Paint | Cumulative shrinkage | Aged strain at break | Aged modulus |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lead white | 0.5% | 0.3–0.8% | ~1 GPa |
| Lead white + litharge | 0.9% | 0.5% | ~2.9 GPa |
| Zinc white | 0.3% | 0.1–0.3% | 2–3 GPa |
| Verdigris | 1.7% | 0.1% | — |
| Red iron oxide | ~0% | 0.3% | ~50 MPa |

  Lead white's strain at break fell from **7.3% at 0.2 years** to under 1% at 31 years[S]. Chalk-glue grounds are modeled with a break strain of **0.002**[V].
- **Layer thicknesses.** A three-layer commercial ground from about 1880 measured **1.5–30 µm (chalk), 5–35 µm and 10–45 µm (lead white)**[V]. Mock-up oil layers measured **59–125 µm for one coat** and 110–188 µm for two[S]. Single paint layers run roughly 10–200+ µm [S; general cross-section ranges, low confidence].
- **Conformal or filling.** That ground is "thicker and smoother, greatly diminishing the texture of the canvas weave"[V]. In the Newtonian free-surface model, thinner films level more slowly at fixed viscosity and wavelength, because τ ∝ h⁻³. At η = 1 Pa·s and σ = 0.035 N/m, λ = 0.3–0.8 mm and h = 10–20 µm give 1/e times of about 0.056–22.5 seconds, which can be fast compared with drying. Whether weave relief survives depends on viscosity, yield stress, contact during application and drying, as well as on film thickness[E].

## 4. Canvas and ground

**Thread counts (plain weave unless noted).** These are measurements of individual paintings, not period averages.

| Canvas | Threads/cm | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| French 18th-century hemp | mostly 12–14 × 9.5–13 | [V] |
| French 18th century, hemp warp and linen weft | 17 × 14 | [V] |
| French 19th century | 10 × 6 (coarse) to 16 × 10 | [V] |
| Twill linen, 1830 | 30 × 29 | [V] |
| Fine linen, 1855 | 38 × 34 | [V] |
| Commercial canvas, 1879/80 | 26.0 × 29.9 | [V] |
| Commercial roll (Tasset et L'Hôte), 1888–90 | ~12 × 15–17 (e.g., 12.3 × 17.3) | [S] |

A usable range for 19th-century canvases is **10–38 threads/cm**, which is a **0.26–1.0 mm pitch**. Warp and weft often differ by 10–40%.

- **Irregularity.** Density along the warp is always more consistent than along the weft[V]. Weft "slubs" (thick spots) are the usual irregularity[S].
- **Cusping (scalloping).** This is "a regular scalloping of the threads at the perimeter" left by the tacks used while the canvas was sized and grounded[V]. On the 1879/80 canvas the original tacks were **5.5–6 cm apart**[V]. Commercial pre-primed rolls often show *no* cusping on edges cut from the roll[V].
- **Ground and texture.** Late-19th-century commercial grounds were either *à grain* (one layer, so more weave texture shows) or *lisse* (two layers, fills the interstices)[S]. An **estimate is 5–40 µm** peak to valley under *à grain* and about 2–10 µm under *lisse* **[E, unverified]**.
- **Mechanics.** Above about 80% RH the canvas *shrinks* as crimp increases, and once dry the glue size, not the canvas, carries the tension[V].

I'm mapping out proportions for sky, mountains, water, and foreground on a 610×457mm canvas, and planning the ground layer — a smooth knife-applied lead white oil ground followed by a thin, broadly-brushed "liquid white" film to paint into wet-on-wet.

Given lead white's long open time, I have the whole session to work wet-on-wet. For the palette, I'm substituting Prussian blue for phthalo blue and relying on vermilion plus white for warm pink tones since there's no true alizarin analog, mixing mountain darks from Prussian blue, bone black, raw umber, and red earth, with foliage darks and highlight greens built from Prussian blue, raw umber, bone black, and chrome yellow.

Before settling further, I should pin down the subject more concretely and check my references on water, tree structure, oil knife work, oil blending, and ground preparation.

{"id": "oil-ground", "title": "Oil ground handling at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## Ground

- An **oil ground** (the default) absorbs nothing: paint stays open and
  glossy longer. An **absorbent ground** (`absorbent=true`) drinks the oil of
  thin paint: matte, lean, quick to set, colors that sit on the surface;
  thick paint stays open and glossy on top, and coarse pigments sink
  further than fine ones. Choose before you start: it is the
  canvas's character.
- A **toned ground** (a little ochre, umber or black in the white) sets the
  middle value from the first stroke; a white ground keeps everything high
  in key and lets thin paint glow.
"}

{"id": "oil-knife", "title": "Knife handling at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## The knife

- `k = knife{width=30}; k:load(p, 1.0); k:lay(points, {pressure={0.5, 0.5}})`
  lays a slab with a flat top, torn where it parts from the blade (its ends,
  its leading edge): light pressure lays it thick, and the paint runs out
  sooner; firm pressure thin, and it goes further. The points set its path.
- Pulled lightly over **dry** impasto, it catches only the ridges: broken
  color over a textured underlayer, a sparkle of light paint on dark.
- `k:scrape(points, {pressure=1})` takes wet paint off down to what is dry:
  to restate a passage, or to leave a ghost of it.
"}

{"id": "tree-structure", "title": "Tree structure and species", "page": 1, "pages": 4, "next_page": 2, "text": "# Trees: how they are built

*A note on how trees grow, branch and taper, from documented sources. "General knowledge" marks statements not tied to a source; "My inference" marks conclusions drawn from sourced facts.*

## In short

1. **A tree is a branching system that grows at its tips and thickens everywhere.** Strong side branches arise mostly near the top of each year's shoot (acrotony). Upright axes build the frame; side axes spread sideways. When a tip dies, the one or more side shoots below it take over, so the axis forks or zigzags.
2. **Diameter is conserved across forks, roughly.** The cross-section below a fork about equals the sum of the cross-sections above it (the branch-area rule). The measured exponent is 1.8–2.3 instead of exactly 2. Every twig is the thin end of a continuous path to the roots.
3. **A side branch is thickest where it leaves its parent.** It is set into the trunk as a sleeve: the branch's own wood turns down and wraps its base as a collar, and trunk wood wraps over that collar every year. A swelling underneath (the branch collar) and usually a raised ridge of bark on top (the branch bark ridge) mark the junction.
4. **Healthy crowns end in a network of long shoots; stressed ones don't.** Roloff's four vitality stages run from a net of long shoots at the crown edge (healthy) to spiky "bottle-brush" tips, then bushy chains of short shoots, then dieback and a shrinking crown.

**Terms used below.** *Acrotony*: side branches strongest near the tip of the parent shoot. *Orthotropic/plagiotropic*: growing upright/growing sideways. *Long shoot/short shoot*: a year's extension that is long and carries branches versus a stubby one. *Epicormic shoot*: a shoot from a dormant bud on an old trunk or limb (German *Wasserreiser*). *Reiteration*: the tree repeating its own basic architecture as a new sub-crown. *Retrenchment*: natural shrinking of an old crown. *Cladoptosis*: a tree's regular shedding of twigs at an abscission layer. *Sapwood/heartwood*: conducting outer wood/non-conducting inner wood.

## 1. How a tree is built

- **Growth rules.** Branches that develop mostly in the distal part of a parent shoot (acrotony) are what give a tree its tree-like rather than bushy habit. Upright (orthotropic) axes "are generally associated with plant skeleton construction." Sideways (plagiotropic) axes explore horizontal space and carry leaves and flowers. If a shoot's tip dies, aborts or turns into a flower, one, two or more branches take over below it (sympodial branching). A string of such takeovers can still look like one straight axis.
- **Limbs, branches, twigs.** Branches carry branches, and those carry twigs; in sympodial trees the steps pile up quickly. **General knowledge:** a mature broadleaved crown commonly has five or more such steps from trunk to this year's twig; I found no source that counts them species by species. Seen from any distance, only the trunk and the first limbs or two read as separate shapes; the finer branching merges into the crown's texture and the ragged edge of its outline.
- **Crowns within the crown.** As a crown matures, big limbs grow crowns of their own, each shaped by where it sits in the tree; this "sequential" reiteration is a normal part of crown construction. After damage, dormant buds produce "traumatic" reiteration: new small crowns on the wounded frame. **General knowledge:** an old crown therefore reads as a few uneven masses, not one even dome.
- **Long shoots and short shoots set the crown edge.** In a vigorous tree the leader and some side shoots at the top are long shoots, making a "network structure" that extends the crown. Next comes a "spikey outline," with bottle-brush tips of long leaders carrying only short side shoots. Then a "short shoot-mode" with "bushy structure, on hold." Last is "retraction mode": "leader die-back, crown reduction". Roloff measured these stages on 100- to 160-year-old beech. He sorts species by life expectancy. Short-lived (80–"}

{"id": "tree-structure", "title": "Tree structure and species", "page": 2, "pages": 4, "next_page": 3, "text": "100 years) includes alder and birch. Medium-lived (150–300) includes beech, spruce, pine and white willow. Long-lived (over 400) includes lime and oak.
- **What distress looks like.** In an ancient tree the outer crown shrinks episodically, and new epicormic shoots grow in the mid and lower crown. Old trees survive through epicormic growth, adventitious rooting, layering and suckering. *My inference:* a crown whose every limb is covered in straight upright shoots reads as a tree reacting to heavy damage or cutting. A healthy mature crown edge is a fine net of long shoots.

## 2. How branches taper and join

- **The branch-area rule.** A mother branch of diameter *d* splitting into daughters *dᵢ* obeys *d*^Δ = Σ *dᵢ*^Δ on average. Measured Δ is between 1.8 and 2.3 for many species (Δ = 2 means cross-sectional area is conserved). *Arithmetic from the rule:* with Δ = 2, two equal daughters are each about 0.71 of the mother's diameter. A daughter with a quarter of the area has half the diameter, and the mother continuing past it drops only to about 0.87 of its former diameter.
- **Why: two explanations.** The *pipe model* (Shinozaki et al. 1964) pictures a tree as a bundle of unit pipes, each connecting a set of leaves to the roots. So the stem area at a height tracks the leaves above it. Below the crown, the pipes of branches long since shed stay in the trunk as "disused pipes." That is why trunks keep thickening toward the base even where no branches remain. Eloy objects that the conducting sapwood can be as little as 5% of a mature trunk's cross-section. He shows instead that the rule follows if a self-similar tree skeleton sizes its diameters to resist wind. Whatever the cause, cross-sections sum roughly at forks.
- **When the rule bends.** Models depart from the rule as side branches get heavier or leave at wider angles. In real branches the departure is small. Beech branches fit a constant-stress design best; fir branches often follow the area rule. *My inference:* a heavy, near-horizontal limb is somewhat thicker at its base than the area rule alone would give.
- **What a junction is.** The cambium runs continuously from trunk to branch. In the upper junction, though, its cells are oriented at "approximately right angles" to the normal direction. Early in the season the branch xylem turns downward at the branch base and "encircles it to form a collar." Later in the season a collar of trunk xylem envelops it. "The branch is structurally attached to the trunk by a […]." Water enters and leaves the branch through the branch collar. Outwardly there is a branch collar on the underside of the branch base and a branch bark ridge on top, running roughly parallel to the branch angle.
- **Why a side branch never starts thinner than it is farther out.** *My inference, from and:* at its base a branch carries the pipes for every leaf beyond it, and each year's collar adds wood there first. Its cross-section therefore shrinks outward, stepwise at each fork and gradually between forks, and never the other way. A branch drawn as a constant-width rod, or narrower where it leaves the trunk, contradicts both.
- **Angle of attachment.** Wide, U-shaped unions are strong. Narrow V-shaped unions "often form included bark," a wedge of inward-rolled bark between two stems. Codominant stems of about equal size from one point often do the same. When a leader is damaged, several branches may become codominant.
- **Dead branches and stubs.** Around a dead branch, the collar and branch bark ridge "continue to grow" and can be told apart from the dead wood. *General knowledge:* over years a living collar can form a sleeve around a dead stub.
- **Twigs end in buds.** Each twig is the current year's shoot and ends in a terminal or false-terminal bud. Buds sit in the leaf scars along it (species details in §3). Nothing in a tree floats. Every twig connects through its parent to the trunk, as the pipe model presumes.

## 3. The species

{"id": "oil-blending", "title": "Blending at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## Blending

- **Blend inside one passage.** Shape the mask like the passage, with its
  edge where the paint already matches. Keep everything you want to keep
  outside the mask, dry shapes included: the blender carries wet paint onto
  them.
- **Look after each pass.** The blender lifts paint as it moves it. When
  darks go pale, texture flattens or the weave shows through, stop.
- **A seam that keeps coming back** needs another method. A smaller patch
  blended again rebuilds the box. Try something else across the whole
  transition on the scratch canvas: a thin tint of the original recipe,
  interlocking strokes of the two neighboring colors over dry paint, or the
  connected passage repainted up to its natural edges.
"}

{"id": "tree-structure", "title": "Tree structure and species", "page": 3, "pages": 4, "next_page": 4, "text": "1 Alder (*Alnus glutinosa*, black alder)

- **Habit.** Short-lived (normally about 60 years, maximum about 160), 10–25 m, on riverbanks, lake shores and marshes. The crown is narrow and upright. Shaded branches die off, so the live crown shrinks relative to the tree. It can be coppiced.
- **Twigs, catkins and cones.** Young twigs are green and sticky. Buds are stalked, purplish brown and somewhat three-sided. Catkins form in autumn and open the next spring. The fruits are small woody "cones" that stay on through winter and release seed gradually.
- **Bark.** Brown and smooth at first, then darker, rough and fissured. Later gray-brown with small broken patches.
- **Damage.** *Phytophthora* disease kills first the fine branches, then the larger ones.

### 3.2 Beech (*Fagus sylvatica*)

- **Habit.** Usually single-stemmed, with silver-gray bark. Typical life span 150–300 years. It keeps growing fast into late maturity and is the most shade-tolerant broadleaf in its range. A stocky trunk and round crown.
- **Twigs and buds.** Twigs are "slender, zigzag, light brown." Buds are long (about 2.5 cm), slender and "widely divergent from stems". Beech was Roloff's model species for the long-shoot/short-shoot vitality stages.
- **Bark.** "Smooth, thin, and dark gray-blue … smooth even on the largest […]". The thin bark protects poorly against fire and stripping.
- **Taper.** Japanese beech branches fit a uniform-stress design best.

### 3.3 Birch (*Betula pendula*, silver; *B. pubescens*, downy)

- **Habit.** Short-lived (commonly 90–100 years, rarely 150), relatively small, with a light canopy. The crown is open and pyramidal, "with distinctly drooping fine branches". In *B. pendula* the branches droop; in *B. pubescens* they grow upward or horizontally.
- **Twigs.** "Slender, reddish brown … noticeably drooping," with slender pointed buds.
- **Bark.** Brown when young, then "silvery-white, with horizontal dark grey lenticels, that with age darkens […]." Young trees show dark scars where shoots dropped. At the base the tree "develops thick bark which splits into narrow, vertical furrows which […]".

### 3.4 Lime (*Tilia cordata*, small-leaved; *T. platyphyllos*, large-leaved)

- **Habit.** 30–40 m, with straight trunks up to about 1 m. Crowns are "quite neat and narrow, becoming untidier as they age," with a branch-free trunk of 10–15 m possible. Both species are largely free of suckers and epicormic growth, unlike the hybrid common lime. Open-grown trees are dense and round, and become as wide as tall.
- **Twigs and buds.** "Slender, zigzag, green-brown or red-tinged (particularly in the winter)." The terminal bud is false; buds are plump with one side bulging.
- **Bark.** Gray or brown, with shallow furrows and flat ridges. "Numerous burls and sprouts often found around the base".
- **Old limes.** They live over 1000 years even when coppiced. Very old stools may have lost their heartwood to rot. Limes were coppiced for long straight poles and can be pollarded.

### 3.5 Oak (*Quercus robur*, pedunculate; *Q. petraea*, sessile)

- **Habit.** In *Q. robur* the main trunk "tends to disappear in the crown, developing irregular boughs with […]." *Q. petraea* usually keeps a main stem with boughs that gradually decrease in size. Heights are usually about 30 m, with diameters up to 1 m. Individuals can live over 1000 years and reach 3–4 m in diameter. The crown is round.
- **Twigs and buds.** Twigs are moderate in thickness and yellow-brown. Buds are "angled, short and round". **General knowledge:** oak buds cluster at the shoot tip, so several shoots start from one point, which gives oak its crooked, clustered branching.
- **Twig shedding (cladoptosis).** In cladoptosis an abscission layer forms and the twig "is shed cleanly," as leaves are. In oak, most shed twigs are one year old and leafless. They fall in autumn and mostly come from vigorously growing trees, so the shedding is not a sign of drought or age. In a 165-"}

{"id": "tree-structure", "title": "Tree structure and species", "page": 4, "pages": 4, "next_page": null, "text": "year-old stand, weak shoots had 27% lower hydraulic conductance, with bottlenecks at nodes and abscission zones.
- **Bark.** Gray and fissured into rectangular elongated blocks, thicker in *Q. robur*. "Deeply fissured with age".
- **Old and damaged oaks.** Oaks coppice and pollard easily. Lateral epicormic shoots leave knots in the wood. Ancient oaks retrench: the crown shrinks through dieback and branch loss ("growing downwards"). The trunk is very wide for the species and very likely hollow, and the tree may live on for centuries. In natural retrenchment, single branches die back while the rest of the crown stays healthy. Serious disease looks different.

### 3.6 Scots pine (*Pinus sylvestris*)

- **Habit.** 23–27 m on average, sometimes over 40 m. It lives 400 years or more. Crowns are rounded when young and round-topped when old. The trunk is often twisted, depending on seed origin. In some conifers, flattening and broadening of the crown may be the only sign of old-age retrenchment.
- **Bark.** The upper stem is "a distinct reddish-orange," while the lower part is "furrowed brown to grey-brown and becomes deeply fissured". "Upper crowns always show orange peeling bark".
- **Needles.** In pairs, twisted.

### 3.7 Norway spruce (*Picea abies*)

- **Habit.** A straight, regular trunk up to 50–60 m, usually living 200–300 years. "The crown is regularly conic, columnar, with whorled, short and […]". Free-standing trees keep green branches down to the ground. Branches are inclined to hanging, as an adaptation to snow load.
- **Branching types.** Young spruces branch in flat "plates" up to about 20 years. After that they develop either the *Plattenfichte* type, with horizontal second-order branches, or the *Kammfichte* ("comb spruce") type, whose second- and higher-order branches hang down like a fringe. A third type is the *Bürstenfichte* ("brush spruce"). Comb spruces dominate on well-supplied sites. Plate spruces dominate on poor bogs and at extreme altitudes.
- **Bark.** Orange-brown. Red-brown and scaly, later gray with flaking scales or plates. Drops of resin are common on trunk and branches.

### 3.8 Willow (white willow, *Salix alba*; other tree willows)

- **The tree.** A fast-growing tree of riverbanks and floodplains, very tolerant of flooding. It "can readily reproduce from suckers or from adventitious roots". The bark is dark gray and deeply fissured with corky ridges. The narrow leaves are silver-gray, and white willow is "cultivated as osiers, characterised by having pliable branches". Medium-lived.
"}

{"id": "oil-glazes", "title": "Glazing and scumbling at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## Glazing and scumbling (over dry paint)

- **Glaze**: a transparent paint (lakes, viridian, ultramarine, a little of
  anything) with plenty of medium (0.7 to 0.85), `hand="glaze"`, over a dry
  passage. It deepens and saturates and lets the light underneath through;
  it rescues a chalky passage. Over impasto it pools in the valleys and
  thins on the ridges, which then shine through. Too much pigment, or any
  white, lays an opaque veil: try it small first. A glaze over the whole
  picture to pull it together has failed more often than it has worked.
- **Scumble**: light paint dragged thin over a dry darker passage, broken
  by the surface. A light load and
  `hand="scumble"` often lay opaque dabs. The veils that blended in came
  from paint thinned with `thinner`, laid in several light passes. Try it
  on the scratch canvas first.
- Glazes and scumbles want the passage under them **dry** (`wait` until
  `drying` says so): over open paint they just mix.
"}

{"id": "oil-impasto", "title": "Impasto handling at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "- Stiff paint holds the brush's marks: blot it (`pile{..., blot=0.3}`) or
  use it as it comes from the tube, with no medium. A full brush lays more with `lay=4`
  to `lay=16`; a coarse hog brush (larger `hair`) leaves coarser ridges.
- In stiff paint the hairs gather into clumps: strokes lie in ridges and
  furrows, walls rise along their sides, a bead where they end. Fluid paint
  levels flat, which suits a glaze.
- Check it with `look` and `mode: "relief"` (raking light from the upper
  left at 25°: it exaggerates, as a raking lamp does) and with
  `mode: "gallery"` (55°, as the picture is seen on a wall). Judge the
  picture under the gallery light; use raking light to inspect the surface.
- Let impasto set before painting into it, unless you want the new stroke
  to drag the old one along.
"}

For the tree silhouette itself, I'm considering filling the shape with short downward-outward hatch strokes, then adding edge strokes for branch tips so the character comes from the branches rather than a flat mask. Since the foreground trees will be large (~600 units tall) and read as dark masses against the glowing sky, the branch structure needs real irregularity: uneven whorl spacing, 2-4 branches per side at varying angles and lengths with occasional gaps, each branch drooping outward then curling up at the tip with a few short hanging fringe strokes like real spruce.

That's thousands of strokes per tree in total, but each is quick so the time cost is manageable. I'm skipping fan-brush strokes since they lay down too thin and translucent for this purpose, and I'm leaning toward building a full scratch study of the composition first so I can judge the large masses before committing to the final painting.

Now I'm sketching out the value plan for the actual canvas: the sky gradient from deep blue at top to a peachy glow concentrated left-of-center, with a few lit cloud streaks and a violet cloud bank upper right; then the far mountain massif slightly left of center with mid-value blue-violet shadows reading against the warmer sky glow.

I'm thinking through alpenglow — the snow faces catching the warm light should be pink-white, while shadow-side snow stays a cool pale blue, since dusk light would pink-tint the peaks. Below that, I'm planning a pale lavender-pink mist band to soften the mountain base into the far shore, then a cooler forested middle-distance ridge with soft treetop texture fading into the haze, possibly layered into two bands of hills at different distances and values.

Next I'm laying out the far shoreline treeline as a dark irregular silhouette broken by a bright waterline, then the mirrored water below with vertical reflections of the mountains and glow plus horizontal light streaks. For the foreground, I'm placing a right-side promontory with tall spruces and bushes over dark rocky land, and a left-side low bank with dry grass, scattered rocks, a couple young spruces, and possibly a weathered dead snag.

I'm weighing composition choices — keeping the lit peak and its reflection as the focal point with the dark right trees framing it, considering whether the big right tree group should overlap and crop part of the mountain range, and deciding to keep a small low bank with reeds on the lower left rather than cutting it entirely for a simpler design. I'm also noting the light direction: sun set to the left, so tree faces on that side would be darker.

Now I'm sketching the overall value distribution — darks around 30%, mids around 45%, lights around 25% — and sequencing the actual painting steps: liquid white base, sky, water base colors, cloud streaks, mountains with knife-applied snow highlights and misting at the base, middle hills, far tree line, then pulling reflections straight down.

    local half = halfw * (0.06 + 0.94 * t^0.85)
    local nb = 1 + math.floor(rand(1, 3.2))
    for side = -1, 1, 2 do
      for j = 1, nb do

          local L = half * rand(0.55, 1.1)
          local x0 = xc(y) + side * rand(0, 2)
          local yy = y + rand(-2, 2)
          local droop = L * rand(0.18, 0.4)

          local nf = math.floor(rand(0, 3.5) * math.min(1, L/20))
          for f = 1, nf do
            local u = rand(0.35, 0.95)
            local fx = x0 + side*L*u
            local fy = yy + droop*u*0.9
            fr:stroke({{fx, fy}, {fx + side*rand(0,2), fy + rand(4, 9) * (0.5 + t)}}, {pressure={0.6, 0.05}})

  local y = top + 2

  while y < base do
    local t = (y - top) / (base - top)
    local half = halfw * (0.05 + 0.95 * t^0.8) * rand(0.65, 1.15)
    local b = (t < 0.25) and fs or f

        n = n + 1

Thinking through the physics: alpenglow means the sun is behind the viewer, so the sky behind the lit peaks would show the cooler atmospheric gradient — the Belt of Venus, a pink band near the horizon with earth's shadow in dusky blue below it, deepening to richer blue higher up.

I'm laying out the composition at 1000x749: sky filling the upper ~470px with the glow centered low-left, then placing the main mountain massif center-right with specific peak coordinates and a ridge extending toward both edges of the frame.

I'm also planning the mist band at the mountain base, a silhouetted spruce tree line along the far shore running mostly on the right side with a gap at left to let the glow reflect in the water, and water reflections of both the glow and the peaks beneath. For the foreground I'm considering dark silhouetted spruces at left against the bright glow for drama, while keeping the mountain peaks as the main focal point.

Working through the water line placement, I realize the peak's reflection would fall offscreen given the current horizon position, so I'm reconsidering the layout — maybe raising the water line to around 480 and limiting the foreground bank to just the bottom corners so the open water stays centered and the mountain's reflection remains visible.

I'm now mapping out tonal values across the scene: the sky ranges from deep blue in the upper right to a pale gold glow near the horizon, while the peaks themselves split into warm lit faces and cooler shadowed ones that read darker than the sky to keep the silhouette legible.

Mid-ground mountain slopes and mist stay muted blue-violet, the far tree line goes nearly black, and the foreground trees and bank anchor the darkest values with ochre grass highlights for contrast. I'm keeping clouds minimal — just one or two warm-lit stratus wisps in the upper left — before moving into the painting order starting with the liquid clear base coat.

Next I'm laying in the sky with crisscross strokes, glow colors first low-left then blues above, blending; tapping in the cloud wisps; then mirroring the sky colors into the water with horizontal strokes aligned to the glow's reflection near the shoreline. After that I'll knife in the far mountains with highlights and lifted mist, add the far tree line, then pull the reflections down vertically before blending horizontal light passes across the water.

I'm weighing whether repeated blending over such a large sky area lifts too much paint each pass, but decide the thin-film removal rate keeps it workable, and the slightly streaky crisscross texture actually suits a soft wet-on-wet sky. For the mountains I'm comparing a brush approach, which leaves gaps showing the sky color, against knife-laid slabs that give denser, more saturated coverage with torn edges along the slope strokes.

Now I'm settling on painting the mountain dark shape with the body hand clipped to the mountain mask and full coverage, then softening with a light blend before adding knife highlights—using a mid-dark bluish value for the base, low-pressure knife strokes for lit faces, and a lighter bluish mix for shadow faces. Since the knife highlight is the key move, I'm sketching out the ridge geometry explicitly, starting from a summit point and tracing the west ridge down to a shoulder to define where those highlight strokes should follow.

I continue mapping the east ridge and the spurs running toward the viewer, treating the left sides of spurs as lit and the right sides as shadow, so the highlight strokes know which faces to travel along. Shorter, lighter strokes break the paint into irregular texture, which is useful for scraped snow on rock—pressure around 0.3-0.4 gives a semi-broken effect. I like the idea of keeping the ridge's top edge crisp like the knife's edge while letting the lower edge tear as the paint runs out, so the blade should sit along the ridge and pull a short distance down the slope.

I'm testing this with a specific ridge segment and computing the blade angle from its direction, then pulling the path down the fall line for about 40 units with light pressure. This confirms that the `angle` parameter represents the blade's own orientation, which aligns with the thin-strip result I saw earlier when angle matched the path direction.

arguments.text:
## Plan (sitting 1)
Subject: a high mountain tarn just after sunset, late autumn, first snow. Glow low-left (sun set to the west, out of frame left); the main peak right of center (~x590,y175) catches the last warm light on its west faces, east faces cool blue-violet. Mist at the mountain base, a far shore of small spruces, still water carrying the glow and the peak's reflection pulled down. Dark spruce group on the right foreground cropping the top; low dark bank with dry grass at bottom-left. Intent: stillness, cold clarity, the last warmth on the heights. Value structure: lightest = lit snow + glow (~220-240), sky mid (~150-185), mountain shadow (~120-140), far trees (~70), foreground trees darkest (~30).
Method: wet-on-wet (alla prima): liquid white (lead white, medium 0.45) over the whole canvas, sky crisscrossed into it and blended, water the same, mountains knife+brush, mist, reflections pulled down, trees with fan, highlights last with blotted paint.

## Scratch trials, day 1 (scratch canvas, oil lead-white ground + liquid white wet)
- Liquid white: pile lead white + medium 0.45, broad hand, coverage 1.5, load 0.5. Stays open. Colors laid into it are lightened by it.
- Sky crisscross: broad hand, load 0.4, coverage 1.3 at +0.7 and again at -0.7 rad, with `piles` weighted by y-functions; then blend(angle 0) x2 over a softened rect: smooth gradient with soft streaky texture; small pale 'holes' remain where the broad strokes missed (accepted as cloud texture, but watch).
- Knife highlight (blotted lead white + vermilion/chrome touch, blot 0.15) over a wet dark knife-laid slab: pressure 0.1-0.32 load 0.4 lays a solid opaque slab that sits on the wet dark without dissolving; 0.4 breaks into horizontal striations; 0.5-0.9 leaves only fine broken lines (a grainy, scraped look). content.thinking:
The snow strokes are too thin, only tracing ridgelines, leaving the mountain looking like a flat blue-gray triangle. I want to build up broader snow masses on the upper lit face using the wider knife to establish a clear lit west face versus shadowed east face, letting the snow define the mountain's planes.

I'm planning the peak's structure: summit at (546,166), with a west ridge dropping to (445,262) and (365,332), an east ridge to (668,264), and a central rib descending toward (520,300) that splits the face into a lit left triangle and a shadowed right triangle, giving the mountain real pyramidal depth. I'll fill the lit triangle with broad snow swaths broken by dark rock ribs along the fall line, and do the same with darker shadow-snow on the opposite face, using low knife pressure for solid slabs.

Increasing pressure toward the end of each stroke breaks the snow up into rock nicely, so I'll angle strokes down the fall line of each face — roughly 115° for the lit side — with the blade turned about 0.9 rad off that path for a wedge-shaped look. I'll extend similar broader shadow-snow fields to the secondary peak and the right shoulder, and add a few dark rib marks afterward if the snow reads too uniform.

content.thinking:
The overall composition works, but the sky needs more depth toward the top, the mountain is too flat and needs atmospheric mist at its base, and the water should be calmer, darker than the sky, and reflect the mountain. Next I want to add mist at the base of the mountain.

The mountain's base stays hidden behind trees and mist, so its reflection mostly shows the dark slopes rather than the summit, which would fall offscreen below the waterline. This creates a nice contrast: warm glow reflected on the lower-left of the water, dark mountain reflected center-right, with foreground spruce silhouettes anchoring the right side.

I'm weighing whether the foreground bank should sit along the bottom-right beneath the spruces, leaving the lower-left open for the glow reflection with maybe a few emergent rocks for accent, or whether a thin shoreline strip should run across the entire bottom. Mapping out the masses — light upper-left and lower-left, dark mountain center-right, darkest spruces framing the right edge — I notice both light areas cluster on the left while the darks dominate the right, which risks feeling left-heavy and asymmetrical.

I'm also picturing the far shore as a low wooded band across the lake with mist rising above it, where tiny spruce silhouettes against the gold glow on the left side would read as a nice delicate accent. For the right side, I'm positioning the two tall spruces and smaller ones so they overlap the main peak's shoulder without fully covering the secondary peak near x 728, keeping it partially visible.

Weighing placement now: trees on the right sit against darker sky for subtler framing, while trees on the left would create dramatic high-contrast silhouettes against the glow but risk blocking that light zone — so the right side would carry the darker mountain and water reflection as the counterbalance instead.

I'm settling on a right-side group of two or three tall spruces (around x 790-1000) with a rocky bank sloping down to the left, ending near x 450 at the bottom edge, leaving the lower-left open as water catching the glow's reflection.

For contrast I'm adding a small distant spruce cluster at the far left edge, silhouetted against the far-shore glow (x 0-180, y 380-470), so the composition reads with tiny trees on the left balanced against the larger near trees on the right.

Now I'm thinking through the mist at the mountain's base — wanting something thinner and more graded than my earlier lumpy test, so I'll scumble a light haze band around y 400-470 with low coverage, strongest near the bottom, using crisscross strokes in a tighter range (y 430-474) before blending it upward into the rest of the scene.

Blending straight into the mountain base with a dry brush would just smear the dark pigment rather than create haze, since there's no light paint underneath to lift — the mountain was painted directly over the sky, so I need to introduce pale mist-colored paint first rather than relying on blending alone. I'm reconsidering the scumble approach from my scratch trial, since laying body paint as a broken veil and letting it mix into the wet paint beneath might give a softer result than a plain blend.

I'll test this on the scratch's water area, painting a fresh dark patch to mimic the mountain base, then try the mist technique side by side to compare before applying it to the real painting.
